headline: A University of Limerick study found that people paid an AI agent presented as female about 10% less than an identical one presented as male.
score_reason: Kept at the pool score: an interesting finding, but a single simulated test reported by one outlet with no journal named.
importance_line: A study suggests workplace gender bias carries over to how people value AI helpers, which matters to women at work first, then firms and designers choosing how AI assistants look and sound, but it is a single simulated test and Gizmodo does not name the journal or say whether it was peer reviewed.
summary: Gizmodo reports on a recently published University of Limerick study in which 189 knowledge workers, working with AI agents in a virtual-reality office, set pay for each agent: they gave the male-presenting “Johan” about 10% more on average than “Johanna”, his identical female-presenting twin, and saw him as more human-like. Only three of the 34 people interviewed afterwards said their behavior could reflect gender bias, although 30 said they would treat the agents the same.
notes: Full text read. No journal, date or authors named by Gizmodo.
